claims.text: Dynamic mechanical behavior in HEAs is controlled by the interplay between dislocation movement and nanoscale fluctuations in local chemical order.
The chemically complex environment in HEAs dynamically pins and releases dislocations during cyclic or high-strain-rate loading.
Dynamic pinning and release of dislocations produces an unusual combination of strength and ductility.
Nanoscale domains of local chemical order arise from the alloy's multicomponent composition.
Local chemical fluctuations act as transient dislocation-pinning sites under dynamic loading.
Pinned dislocations subsequently depin through thermally activated or strain-rate-induced processes.
Pinning and depinning modulate resistance to dislocation motion.
Modulation of dislocation resistance enhances strain hardening while maintaining ductility.
HEAs will exhibit a higher strain-hardening rate than conventional single-phase alloys lacking comparable multicomponent chemical complexity.
HEAs will exhibit a more pronounced yield point followed by a stress-strain plateau than the conventional-alloy baseline during dynamic loading.
The predicted behavior will be most detectable at intermediate strain rates and moderate temperatures.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to single-phase HEAs at moderate deformation rates and temperatures.
The hypothesis may not apply to multiphase HEAs.
At very low or high temperatures or extreme strain rates, additional deformation mechanisms may dominate.
Direct observations correlating local chemical order with dislocation pinning during dynamic loading in HEAs are scarce.
